doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Teaching as her calling
summary: Music was never a choice; she taught about twelve years, tried to quit, and found her home teaching high school choral music.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Was there a point that you can remember where you made a conscious sort of career decision about — okay music’s definitely in me. Now what am I going to do with it?

Okay. I didn’t have that choice. Okay? Talking about a career decision. It had to be music. It was music. I feel that my calling is to teach it. Okay? Performing — that’s the bonus side of it. But my calling is to teach. Therefore that’s where my commitment has been, to teaching, teaching, teaching. Now what I learned in performing I bring to the classroom. What I learn in the classroom I bring to performing you see. But teaching is the thing that I really believe that I’ve been called to do. And I tried to stop, I tried to stop. I taught for about twelve years and I said I don’t want to do this anymore. I don’t want to be in the classroom anymore. I’ll just go on and do the gigs. But there was something missing so I started teaching privately, teaching at home. But it still was not enough. Then I got a call to go to the school where I am now and as soon as I walked in the classroom I said —
What grade levels do you teach?
Nine through twelve. High school. And it was just like a good deep sigh, whew.

And I love teaching choral music, I really do. But that’s what it’s turned out to be. But I can still do the gigs you see. I can still sing with the choirs. But I still have — because again, as I said, what I learn in performing I bring back to the classroom. Because certainly maybe something that you saw me doing this evening, had I not been a performer I would not have been able to bring that kind of punch. You know what I’m saying?

Um hum. Absolutely. And it makes you, especially if your students can see you perform on occasion, I think it really makes you legitimate in their eyes and gives way to what you pass on to them. And you don’t have to depend on gigs to pay the rent.
